name: CUTLASS collective GEMM: the arch-tagged Tensor Core mainloop that most production GEMM kernels wrap
arithmetic_intensity: A GEMM at batch B is memory-bound below the ridge point and compute-bound above it; a tile-based mainloop does not change that crossover, it changes how close a real kernel gets to it. What CUTLASS's collective mainloop actually reduces is shared-memory traffic per FLOP: a tile of size BM x BN x BK re-reads each operand element once per tile traverse rather than once per output element, so HBM bytes per FLOP falls as 1/BN (for A) and 1/BM (for B). Tile size is bounded by the hardware: on Hopper the extended static shared memory is 228 KB per CTA (PTX ISA) versus the 48 KB per-CTA static default, which is what permits the large Hopper tiles; CUTLASS lists 328 KB shared-memory allocations for Blackwell-class targets. Register pressure bounds the other side - accumulator tiles live in registers (Hopper WGMMA) or in tensor memory (Blackwell tcgen05), and that choice determines how many pipeline stages fit before spilling.
workarounds: Stage the mainloop with async copies so HBM->SMEM overlaps MMA (cp.async on Ampere+, cp.async.bulk/TMA on Hopper+)

Arch-specific target flags: Hopper and Blackwell PTX instructions are 'architecture-accelerated features' requiring sm_90a or sm100a - building them for the base sm_90 or sm_100 target silently loses the acceleration
Blackwell path uses umma/tcgen05 with tensor-memory accumulators; Hopper path uses wgmma with register accumulators
Blockscaled (MXFP4/NVFP4/MXFP8) GEMM kernels and 2:4 sparsity for FP4 as separate kernels rather than flags on the dense kernel
notes: This is the mechanism layer underneath Marlin, Machete, DeepGEMM and most hand-written GEMMs: those libraries are usually a CUTLASS collective builder plus a custom epilogue or a custom operand layout, not a new GEMM algorithm. The single most decision-relevant fact in CUTLASS's README is a portability trap: 'The NVIDIA Blackwell SM100 architecture used in the datacenter products has a different compute capability than the one underpinning NVIDIA Blackwell GeForce RTX 50 series GPUs (SM120). As a result, kernels compiled for Blackwell SM100 architecture with arch conditional features (using sm100a) are not compatible with RTX 50 series GPUs.' So a datacenter Blackwell and a consumer Blackwell are different kernel targets, and a kernel library that only ships sm100a paths leaves SM120 parts on an older path. CUTLASS 3.0 introduced CuTe (layout/tensor abstractions over threads and data); 4.0 released the CuTe DSL, a Python kernel DSL whose kernels are written in Python, lower to PTX, and are claimed to cut compile times 20-30x versus C++ templates. Blackwell entries also list extended tensor memory from 512 to 576 columns and higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) MMA instructions. Perf figures in the README are NVIDIA's own.
